rows.description: A stranger says "come, I have sweets" or "your mother sent me". I feel tempted or confused. Wise rule: say no, run to a trusted adult and tell. A grown-up who asks a child for help or secrecy is a warning sign.
A visiting uncle says "give me a kiss" and my parent says I must. I feel uncomfortable. A wise parent respects a child's "no" to hugs and offers a wave or high five. My body belongs to me.

A shopkeeper helps me when I am lost in the market and calls my parents. I learn some strangers are safe helpers, such as a shop owner, a police officer or a mother with children. Knowing whom to ask keeps me safe.

A stranger at the market speaks to me and I hide behind Mummy. This fear is healthy. I feel safe near my parent. Wise adults teach that a polite hello is fine near them but I should never go off with anyone.
When my idol is criticised I defend them fiercely, even when the criticism is fair. Wise: loyalty to a person should not switch off my own judgment.
Treats the idol as flawless and defends every act; healthy admiration keeps the ability to disagree and see the person as human.
Fans of rival stars abuse each other online and I join in. Wise: notice how it feels good to belong and hurts real people; step out when it turns cruel.
A creator sells expensive courses or betting apps to young fans. Recognise it: trust built on likes can be monetised. Check claims and never spend what isn't mine.

My in-laws use guilt, hints, or family reputation to steer our choices and I feel cornered. I stay calm, keep decisions with my partner, and speak united; I need not win an argument to hold my ground.

My partner and my parents are in conflict and I feel pulled apart. I stay loyal to my marriage while treating my parents with respect, refuse to carry tales between them, and do not make my partner the villain.

My partner's family disapproves of me because of my caste, region, job, or background and I feel hurt and small. Their prejudice is not my worth. I stay courteous, let my partner speak up, and let time and conduct do their work.

I quietly resent my partner's family for intruding and comparing me to others. I share this with my partner without attacking their parents, and we agree on boundaries together; bottled resentment leaks out as coldness.

Family WhatsApp groups turn every festival into a political fight. You may love them and still be exhausted by forwards. Set gentle rules: no forwards, verify before sharing, change the subject warmly, or mute without drama.

A relative or colleague praises a leader you distrust, and heat rises. Mature action: ask what worries them, find shared facts, and disengage when it turns to insults. Winning the argument seldom changes a mind or protects a relationship.

Volunteering for a movement gives energy and friends. Good: canvassing honestly, listening to voters, and knowing your limits. Watch for slogans replacing thinking and for excusing your side's wrongs.

You admire a leader and feel part of a cause. Support can be sincere, but keep the ability to criticise. Treating leaders as infallible turns citizens into followers, and disagreement on specific acts is not betrayal.

An ex-member shares that she felt the same fears and now finds peace. I feel less alone. Wise: listen without rushing the decision and take one safe step at a time. Harmful: replacing one authority with another.
I am asked to donate, hand over my phone and stop seeing old friends "for my growth". Wise: these are control signals; keep independent contact, money and a way to leave, and talk to someone outside.

My friend joined a group I find worrying, and I want to rescue him. Wise: keep contact, ask open questions, avoid mocking, and share information gently. Harmful: pressure or secret plots that prove the group right.

My family begs me to leave the group, and I see them as enemies who do not understand. Wise: listen for love inside their fear, and keep one connection alive even if I disagree. Harmful: cutting them off as told.

My friend plays with a new girl and I feel a burning in my chest. I say "she is not allowed to play". Wise action: say "I felt sad" and invite both to play. Excluding someone to keep a friend is the harmful pattern.
My friend says "you are my best friend" and saves me a seat. I feel special and secure. I learn friendship means being chosen and choosing back, and I try to be kind and keep secrets kindly.
I like the girl next to me and ask "do you want to play?" My heart is thumping but she says yes. I feel brave and happy. Making the first move kindly, even shyly, is the start of friendship.

I cry when my best friend is absent and will not play with anyone else. Close attachment is sweet but I also need other friends. A wise adult helps me to join a small group so my world does not depend on one child.
